en: Dīgha Nikāya 25:
The Udumbarika Sutta 1.
The Account of the Wanderer Nigrodha
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Now at that time, the wanderer Nigrodha was residing in the Udumbarikā Wanderers’ Park together with a large assembly of wanderers, numbering about three hundred.
Then, in the middle of the day, the householder Sandhāna departed from Rājagaha to see the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the householder Sandhāna:
"It is the wrong time to see the Blessed One."
The Blessed One was in seclusion;
it was not the time for visiting the bhikkhus who were esteemed by the mind.
The bhikkhus who were esteemed by the mind were also in seclusion.
"What if I were to go to the Udumbarikā Park, to where the wanderer Nigrodha is?
Then the householder Sandhāna went to the Udumbarikā Park, to where the wanderer Nigrodha was.
Now at that time, the wanderer Nigrodha was seated together with a large assembly of wanderers who were making a great noise and a loud clamor, engaged in various kinds of worldly chatter.
That is to say: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers,
talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drinks, talk of clothes, talk of beds, talk of garlands, talk of perfumes, talk of relatives,
talk of vehicles, talk of villages, talk of towns, talk of cities, talk of districts, talk of women, and talk of heroes.
"Talk about streets, talk about wells, talk about ancestors, talk about diversity, talk about the origin of the world, talk about the origin of the ocean,
or talk about 'thus it was' and 'thus it will be'.
Then the wanderer Nigrodha saw the householder Sandhāna coming from afar.
Seeing his own assembly, he quieted them, saying:
"Be silent, sirs; do not make a noise.
This disciple of the ascetic Gotama, the householder Sandhāna, is coming."
"Furthermore, among the white-robed lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama residing in Rājagaha, this householder Sandhāna is one of them.
These venerable ones desire little noise, are disciplined in regard to little noise, and speak in praise of little noise.
It would be well if, perceiving that the assembly is quiet, he might think it fit to approach."
When this was said, those wanderers became silent.
Then the householder Sandhāna approached the wanderer Nigrodha; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the wanderer Nigrodha.
After exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Sandhāna said this to the wanderer Nigrodha:

“Indeed, these venerable wanderers of other sects, having gathered and assembled together, dwell noisy, making loud and great clamor, devoted to various kinds of worldly talk, such as talk of kings...
[and so on] ... or talk of ‘thus it was’ and ‘thus it will be.

But that Blessed One otherwise resorts to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats—places that are quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, hidden away from men, and suitable for seclusion.”
When this was said, the wanderer Nigrodha said this to the householder Sandhāna:
"Come now, householder, you should know: with whom does the ascetic Gotama converse? With whom does he engage in discussion? With whom does he engage in the lucidity of wisdom?
The ascetic Gotama’s wisdom is fit for empty places; the ascetic Gotama is one who frequents no assemblies; he is not fit for conversation."
Thus he frequents only the remote outskirts.
Just as a one-eyed cow that wanders along the edge frequents only the remote outskirts,
even so the wisdom of the ascetic Gotama is fond of empty places.
The ascetic Gotama does not move in society;
he is not fit for conversation.
He frequents only the most remote places.
"Come now, householder, let the ascetic Gotama come to this assembly; with a single question we shall overwhelm him, and I think we shall hold him back like an empty jar.
The Blessed One, with his purified divine ear-element, which surpasses that of humans, heard this conversation between the householder Sandhāna and the wanderer Nigrodha.

Then the Blessed One, having descended from Vulture Peak Mountain, approached the Peacock Sanctuary on the bank of the Sumāgadhā River. Having arrived, he walked back and forth in the open air at the Peacock Sanctuary on the bank of the Sumāgadhā.
Nigrodha the wanderer saw the Blessed One walking back and forth in the open air at the Peacock Sanctuary on the bank of the Sumāgadhā.
Upon seeing him, he quieted his own assembly:
“Sirs, be quiet; do not make a noise, sirs. This ascetic Gotama is walking back and forth in the open air at the Peacocks’ Feeding Ground on the bank of the Sumāgadhā.
That venerable one is fond of quiet and speaks in praise of quiet.
Perhaps, seeing that the assembly is quiet, he might think it fit to approach.”
“If the ascetic Gotama were to come to this assembly, we would ask him this question:

‘Venerable sir, what is that Dhamma of the Blessed One by which the Blessed One trains his disciples, and by which the disciples, being trained by the Blessed One, claim to have attained consolation and the fundamental goal of the holy life?
When this was said, those wanderers became silent.
2. The Discourse on the Loathing of Austerity Then the Blessed One approached the wanderer Nigrodha.
Then the wanderer Nigrodha said this to the Blessed One:
“Come, Bhante, welcome, Bhante! It has been long, Bhante, since the Blessed One made this occasion to come here.
Let the Blessed One sit down; this seat is prepared.”
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
The wanderer Nigrodha also took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to the wanderer Nigrodha:
“Nigrodha, for what discussion are you gathered here now, and what was the conversation of yours that was left unfinished?
When this was said, the wanderer Nigrodha said this to the Blessed One:
“Just now, Bhante, we saw the Blessed One walking back and forth in the open air at the Peacock Sanctuary on the bank of the Sumāgadhā River. Having seen him, we spoke thus:”
“If the ascetic Gotama were to come to this assembly, we would ask him this question:

‘Venerable sir, what is that Dhamma of the Blessed One by which the Blessed One trains his disciples, and by which the disciples, being trained by the Blessed One, claim to have attained consolation and the fundamental purpose of the holy life?
Venerable sir, this was our conversation that remained unfinished when the Blessed One arrived.”

“Nigrodha, it is difficult for you— who hold a different view, who accept a different doctrine, who find pleasure in a different doctrine, who employ a different practice, and who follow a different teacher—
to understand that by which I train my disciples, and by which my trained disciples claim to have attained consolation regarding the fundamental basis of the holy life.”
“Come now, Nigrodha, ask me a question regarding your own teacher’s doctrine of self-disgust:
‘Venerable sir, in what way is austerity and self-disgust fulfilled, and in what way is it unfulfilled?
When this was said, those wanderers became noisy, making a loud clamor and a great din:

“It is wonderful, indeed, sir! It is marvelous, indeed, sir! Such is the great psychic power and great majesty of the ascetic Gotama, that he can set aside his own doctrine and engage in debate with the doctrine of another!
Then Nigrodha the wanderer, having silenced those wanderers, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, we are teachers of austerity and self-reproach; we dwell devoted to austerity and self-reproach, making austerity and self-reproach our core.”
“Venerable sir, how is it that asceticism and self-disgust are fulfilled, and how are they unfulfilled?

“In this case, Nigrodha, an ascetic is naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands, not coming when asked, not staying when asked; he does not accept food brought to him, nor food specially prepared for him, nor an invitation;

he does not accept food from the mouth of a pot, nor from the mouth of a basket, nor across a threshold, nor from between two people eating, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing a child, nor from a woman living with a man, nor from where a dog is waiting, nor from where flies are swarming.”

There is no intervening staff, nor an intervening pestle; he does not eat while two others are eating; he does not eat from a pregnant woman, nor from a nursing woman, nor from a woman who has gone to a man;
he does not eat in crowds, nor where she is present, nor where flies are swarming;
he does not drink fish, meat, liquor, fermented spirits, or grain-beer.

He becomes one who goes for alms at a single house and eats a single morsel, or one who goes for alms at two houses and eats two morsels, up to one who goes for alms at seven houses and eats seven morsels; he subsists on a single gift, or subsists on two gifts, or subsists on as many as seven gifts;
he takes food once a day, or takes food once every two days, or takes food once every seven days—thus he dwells engaged in the practice of taking meals by turn, even for a period of half a month.
Thus he subsists on either millet, or wild rice, or wild barley,
or water chestnuts, or hemp seeds, or rice bran, or the scum of boiled rice, or oil-cake, or grass, or cow dung;
he maintains himself by feeding on forest roots and fruits, eating only what has fallen of its own accord.
Thus he wears hempen robes, he wears robes of hemp-mixed cloth, he wears shrouds from cemeteries, he wears rag-robes, he wears bark-fiber garments,
he wears antelope skins, he wears strips of antelope skin, he wears grass-cloth garments, he wears bark-cloth garments,
he wears wooden-shield garments, he wears hair-blankets, and he wears wool-blankets made of animal fur.
He wears [clothing], he even wears an owl’s wing;
he is one who plucks out his hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out his hair and beard;
he is one who stands continuously, rejecting the use of a seat.
He is one who squats, devoted to the practice of squatting;
he is one who uses a bed of thorns, spreading his bed upon a bed of thorns;
he also makes his bed on a wooden plank, or he makes his bed on the bare ground.
He is one who uses a single garment,
wears dust and dirt,
and dwells in the open air.
He is one who uses whatever seat is provided;
he is also one who eats only what is left over, devoted to the practice of eating such remnants;
he is also one who abstains from drinks, devoted to the practice of not drinking.
He dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water for a third time each evening.
What do you think, Nigrodha,
if this is so, is his austerity and self-disgust fulfilled or unfulfilled?”
“Certainly, Bhante, when this is so, the asceticism of self-disgust is fulfilled, not unfulfilled.
“But even with such fulfillment of the asceticism of self-disgust, Nigrodha, I say there are many kinds of defilements. 2.1.
Defilements (Upakkilesa)
“But how, venerable sir, does the Blessed One speak of various defilements in relation to such complete austerity and self-disgust?
“In this case, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes an ascetic practice; he becomes elated by that austerity and his intention is fulfilled.
That an ascetic undertakes an ascetic practice and becomes elated by that austerity and has his intention fulfilled—this, Nigrodha, is one kind of defilement.”
This too, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity; by means of that austerity, he exalts himself and disparages others.
That an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity and, by means of that austerity, exalts himself and disparages others—this too, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the ascetic.
This too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for an ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity, and through that austerity he becomes intoxicated, infatuated, and falls into negligence.
That an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity, and through that austerity he becomes intoxicated, infatuated, and falls into negligence—this too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for an ascetic.
This too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for an ascetic.

Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes asceticism; by means of that asceticism, he produces gain, honor, and renown. He becomes elated by that gain, honor, and renown, his purpose being fulfilled.

That an ascetic undertakes asceticism and, by means of that asceticism, produces gain, honor, and renown, and becomes elated by that gain, honor, and renown with his purpose fulfilled—this too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for an ascetic.
This too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for an ascetic.

Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes asceticism; by means of that asceticism, he produces gain, honor, and fame. Because of that gain, honor, and fame, he exalts himself and disparages others.

That an ascetic undertakes asceticism, and by means of that asceticism produces gain, honor, and fame, and because of that gain, honor, and fame exalts himself and disparages others—this too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for an ascetic.
This too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for an ascetic.

Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity; through that austerity he produces gain, honor, and renown. He becomes intoxicated by that gain, honor, and renown; he becomes infatuated with it and falls into negligence.

That an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity, and through that austerity produces gain, honor, and renown, and then becomes intoxicated by that gain, honor, and renown, becomes infatuated with it and falls into negligence—this too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for an ascetic.
This, Nigrodha, is also an affliction for an ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic becomes fastidious regarding food, thinking:
"This suits me; this does not suit me."
Thus, whatever he does not approve of, he abandons with longing;
but whatever he approves of, he consumes while being attached to it, infatuated with it, and clinging to it, seeing neither the danger in it nor the wisdom for its transcendence...
This too, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes the practice of austerity for the sake of craving for gain, honor, and renown, thinking:
‘Kings, royal ministers, kshatriyas, brahmins, householders, and members of other sects will honor me.
… This too, Nigrodha, is a defilement of the ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic disparages a certain ascetic or brahmin, saying:
“Why does this one, living in abundance, consume all kinds of food? That is to say:

root-propagated plants, stem-propagated plants, joint-propagated plants, crown-propagated plants, and fifthly, seed-propagated plants; even those split by lightning or gnawed by the tips of teeth, he consumes under the pretext of being an ascetic. … [and so on] …
This too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for an ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic sees another ascetic or brahmin being honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped by families.
Having seen this, it occurs to him:
‘They indeed honor, revere, respect, and worship this person who lives on many things from families;
yet they do not honor, revere, respect, or worship me, though I am an ascetic living a life of austerity,’ thus he gives rise to envy and avarice toward families...
This too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for an ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic sits right in front of people...
This too, Nigrodha, is an imperfection in an ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic goes among families, making a display of himself:
‘This too is my austerity, this too is my austerity,’ ... [and so on] ... Nigrodha, this too is a defilement of the ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic indulges in some form of concealment.
When asked, “Do you approve of this? if he does not approve, he says, “I approve”;
if he approves, he says, “I do not approve.
Thus, he speaks a deliberate lie … [as before] …
This too, Nigrodha, is a corruption of an ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, when a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata is teaching the Dhamma, an ascetic does not acknowledge a valid argument that ought to be acknowledged...
This too, Nigrodha, is a corruption of an ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic may be prone to anger and resentment.
That an ascetic is prone to anger and resentment,
Nigrodha, is also an impurity in an ascetic.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic is one who is contemptuous and insolent … [as before] … he is envious and stingy … he is fraudulent and deceitful …
He is stubborn and arrogant;
he has evil desires and is under the sway of evil wishes;
he holds wrong view and is possessed by a view that clings to extremes.
"He is one who clings to his own views, holds them tenaciously,
and is reluctant to relinquish them. Nigrodha, that a practitioner of austerity is one who clings to his own views, holds them tenaciously,
and is reluctant to relinquish them— this too, Nigrodha, is an affliction for the practitioner of austerity."
“What do you think, Nigrodha, are these defilements of asceticism and self-mortification defilements or non-defilements?
“Certainly, Bhante, these are defilements of asceticism and self-mortification; they are not non-defilements.”
"It is indeed possible, Bhante, that some ascetic here might be possessed of all these defilements;
what need is there to mention him being possessed of only one or another of them?
2.2. Discussion on Reaching the Pure Sprout Stage.
“Here, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity; yet because of that austerity, he is not satisfied and his intention is not fulfilled.
Insofar as an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity and, because of that austerity, is neither satisfied nor has his intention fulfilled—in this respect, he is pure in that matter.”
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity; by that austerity he does not exalt himself nor disparage others...
In this way, he is pure in that respect.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity; by that austerity he is not intoxicated, infatuated, or falls into negligence... [and so on].
In this way, he is pure in that respect.

Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic undertakes a practice of austerity; through that austerity, he produces gain, honor, and fame. Yet, because of that gain, honor, and fame, he is not satisfied and his purpose is not fulfilled...
[as before] ...in this way, he is pure in that respect.

In this way, he is pure in that regard.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic does not become fastidious regarding food, thinking:
"This suits me; this does not suit me."
Thus, whatever is not pleasing to him, he abandons without regard for it;
but whatever is pleasing to him, he uses without attachment, without infatuation, and without being consumed by passion, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape.
In this way, he is pure in that respect.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic does not undertake the practice of austerity for the sake of craving for gain, honor, and renown, thinking:
‘Kings, royal ministers, kshatriyas, brahmins, householders, and members of other sects will honor me.
... In this way, he is pure in that regard.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic does not disparage some other recluse or brahmin, saying:
“Why does this man, who lives on many kinds of food, eat everything? That is to say:
root-crops, stem-crops, joint-crops, tip-crops, and fifthly, seed-crops; he is like a thunderbolt, a toothpick, according to the recluse’s own proclamation. …pe…
In this way, he is pure in that respect.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic sees another ascetic or brahmin being honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped among families.
Having seen this, it does not occur to him:
‘They indeed honor, revere, respect, and worship this person who lives on many kinds of livelihood among families;
yet they do not honor, revere, respect, or worship me, though I am an ascetic living a life of austerity,’ thinking thus, he does not give rise to envy or stinginess regarding families...
In this way, he is pure in that regard.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic does not sit within sight [of the laity]...
in this way he is pure in that respect.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic does not wander among families while making himself known:
‘This too is my austerity, this too is my austerity’ … [as before] … in this way he is pure in that regard.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, an ascetic does not indulge in anything at all that is concealed; he thinks:
When asked, "Does this agree with you?", he said "It does not agree" regarding what did not agree;
and he said [the same] regarding what did agree.
"It is acceptable.
Thus he does not speak a deliberate lie...
In this way, he is pure in that regard.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, when a practitioner of asceticism is teaching the Dhamma to a Tathāgata or a disciple of a Tathāgata, he approves of the method that is indeed correct and worthy of approval...
In this way, he is pure in that respect.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, the practitioner of asceticism is free from anger and free from enmity.
In this way too, Nigrodha, a practitioner of asceticism who is free from anger and free from malice is pure in that respect.
Furthermore, Nigrodha, a practitioner of asceticism is free from denigration and free from disparagement...
[and so on] ...he is free from envy and free from avarice.
He is not fraudulent and not deceitful;
he is not stubborn and not conceited;
he does not have evil desires and is not under the sway of evil desires.
He does not hold wrong view, nor is he possessed of views that grasp at extremes… He does not cling to his own views as supreme, nor is he obstinate in his grip on them,
but is ready to relinquish them. And this, Nigrodha, is how an ascetic does not cling to his own views as supreme, is not obstinate in his grip on them, and is ready to relinquish them.
"In this way, he is pure in that regard.
What do you think, Nigrodha,
if this is so, is asceticism through self-disgust pure or impure?"
“Surely, venerable sir, when this is so, asceticism through self-disgust is pure and not impure; it has reached the summit and reached the core.
“Nigrodha, it is not by this much that asceticism through self-disgust has reached the summit and reached the core;
rather, it has only reached the bark.”
2.3. The Discussion on Attaining Purified Mindfulness “But to what extent, venerable sir, does austerity and self-disgust reach the peak and reach the essence?
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would cause me to reach the very peak and the very essence of austerity and self-disgust.”
“Here, Nigrodha, an ascetic is restrained by the fourfold restraint.
And how, Nigrodha, is an ascetic restrained by the fourfold restraint?
Here, Nigrodha, an ascetic does not take life, does not cause another to take life, and does not approve of one who takes life.”
He does not take what is not given, nor does he cause another to take what is not given, nor does he approve of one who takes what is not given.
He does not speak falsehood, nor does he cause another to speak falsehood, nor does he approve of one who speaks falsehood.
He does not covet what is cultivated [by others], nor does he cause another to covet what is cultivated, nor does he approve of one who covets what is cultivated.
In this way, Nigrodha, an ascetic is restrained by the fourfold restraint.
When, Nigrodha, an ascetic is restrained by the fourfold restraint, that constitutes his asceticism.
He strives for the higher and does not revert to the lower.
Thus he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a jungle-thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Having returned from his almsround after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly calmed; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he dwells, pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness. Likewise the second quarter; likewise the third.

In the same way, the fourth [direction]. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
With a mind imbued with compassion... [and so on].
With a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy …pe… he dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity. Likewise the second; likewise the third;
likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity.
“He dwells having pervaded with a mind that is vast, exalted, immeasurable, and free from enmity and ill will.
What do you think, Nigrodha:
if this is so, is his austerity and self-disgust pure or impure?”
“Certainly, venerable sir, when that is so, asceticism through self-disgust is pure and not impure; it has reached the peak and reached the core.
“Nigrodha, it is not by this much alone that asceticism through self-disgust has reached the peak and reached the core;
rather, it has only reached the bark.”
2.4. Discussion on the Attainment of Pure Pith “But to what extent, Bhante, does austerity and self-reproach reach the summit and reach the core?
It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would lead me to the very summit of austerity and self-reproach, and lead me to its very core.”
“Here, Nigrodha, an ascetic is restrained by the fourfold restraint.
And how, Nigrodha, is an ascetic restrained by the fourfold restraint?
… [as above] … When, Nigrodha, an ascetic is restrained by the fourfold restraint, that constitutes his asceticism.”
Thus he strives and does not turn back toward the inferior.
He resorts to a secluded lodging...
having abandoned these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, [he dwells].
With a mind imbued with loving-kindness …pe… with a mind imbued with compassion …pe… with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy …pe…
He dwells having pervaded [the world] with a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
He recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say:
one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births...
For forty births, for fifty births, for a hundred births, for a thousand births, for a hundred thousand births, for many aeons of world-contraction,
for many aeons of world-expansion, and for many aeons of both contraction and expansion, [he recollects: "In that place I had such a name,
such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan."
"Having passed away from there, I arose there; there I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
having passed away from there, I have reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
“What do you think, Nigrodha, if this were so, would that austerity and self-disgust be pure or impure?
“Certainly, Bhante, if this were so, that austerity and self-disgust would be pure, not impure; it would have reached the summit and reached the essence.”
“Not by this much alone, Nigrodha, does austerity and self-disgust reach the summit and reach the core;
rather, it has reached only the sapwood.
3. The Discourse on Reaching the Summit and the Core of Purification.
“But to what extent, Bhante, does asceticism through self-disgust reach its peak and reach its core?

It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would lead me to the very peak and the very core of asceticism through self-disgust. “In this case, Nigrodha, an ascetic is restrained by the fourfold restraint. What four? Here, Nigrodha, an ascetic refrains from eating at night, refrains from eating at the wrong time, refrains from accepting gold and silver, and refrains from accepting raw grain and raw meat. To this extent, Nigrodha, asceticism through self-disgust reaches its peak and reaches its core.”
And how, Nigrodha, is an ascetic restrained by the fourfold restraint? ...
[as before] ... When, Nigrodha, an ascetic is restrained by the fourfold restraint, that constitutes his asceticism.
He strives for the higher, and does not revert to what is inferior.
Thus he resorts to a secluded lodging...
having abandoned these five hindrances, which are defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, he dwells with a mind imbued with loving-kindness... [and so on].
He dwells having pervaded the mind with an awareness accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.

He recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births... thus, with their aspects and particulars, he recollects his manifold past abodes.
Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—
inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings pass on according to their kamma:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct of body, possessed of misconduct of speech, and possessed of misconduct of mind..."
They were possessed of [these qualities], revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong views, and undertaking actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these worthy beings were possessed of good conduct of body, possessed of good conduct of speech, and possessed of good conduct of mind.
‘They do not revile the noble ones; they hold right view and undertake actions based on right view.

With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate.
He understands beings according to their karma.
What do you think, Nigrodha,
if this is so, is that austerity and self-reproach pure or impure?”
“Certainly, Bhante, this being so, the asceticism of self-disgust is pure and not impure; it has reached the summit and reached the essence.
“To this extent, Nigrodha, the asceticism of self-disgust has reached the summit and reached the essence.
Thus, Nigrodha, as for what you said to me:”

“Venerable sir, what indeed is that Dhamma of the Blessed One by which the Blessed One trains his disciples, and by which the disciples, being trained by the Blessed One, claim to have attained consolation and the underlying intention of the beginning of the holy life?

“In this way, Nigrodha, that ground is more excellent and more sublime—that by which I train my disciples, and by which my disciples, being trained by me, claim to have attained consolation and the underlying intention of the beginning of the holy life.
When this was said, those wanderers became noisy, making a loud clamor and a great din:
“In this we have failed, along with our teacher; we know nothing further beyond this.
4. Nigrodha’s Meditation:
When the householder Sandhāna knew this:
“Indeed, these wanderers of other sects are now eager to hear the Blessed One’s words; they lend an ear and apply their minds to understand.
Then he said this to the wanderer Nigrodha:
“Thus, venerable Nigrodha, as for what you said to me:”
“Come now, householder, you should know this: with whom does the ascetic Gotama converse? With whom does he engage in discussion? With whom does he achieve clarity of wisdom?
The wisdom of the ascetic Gotama is suited for empty places; the ascetic Gotama does not frequent assemblies and is not fit for conversation;
he frequents only the most remote corners, just as a one-eyed cow that wanders along the edge keeps to the very extremities.”
"In the same way, the wisdom of the ascetic Gotama is acquired in empty dwellings; the ascetic Gotama does not frequent assemblies and is not fit for conversation.

He frequents only the most remote places. Come now, householder, let the ascetic Gotama come to this assembly; with a single question we shall overwhelm him, and I think we shall contain him like an empty jar.
"Venerable sir, that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One has arrived here; yet he does not frequent assemblies."
“Make him a cow-eared ox; make him wander along the edge of the herd; make him collapse with a single question; and make him sink down like an empty jar.
When this was said, the wanderer Nigrodha sat silent, crestfallen, with shoulders drooping and head bowed, brooding and speechless.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the wanderer Nigrodha was silent, crestfallen, with drooping shoulders and bowed head, brooding and speechless, said this to the wanderer Nigrodha:
“Is it true, Nigrodha, that these words were spoken by you?
“It is true, Bhante; these words were spoken by me as one who is foolish, deluded, and unskilled.
“What do you think, Nigrodha?”
"Have you heard from the wandering ascetics who are aged, elderly, and teachers of teachers, as they speak:

‘Those who were in the past Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones—did those Blessed Ones, having gathered and assembled together, dwell making a clamor, a loud noise, and a great din, devoted to various kinds of frivolous talk? That is to say:
talk of kings, talk of thieves... [and so on] ...or talk of whether things will be thus or will not be?’"
“Are those Blessed Ones now living in forest groves and remote lodgings— places of little sound,
little noise, secluded from people, hidden from men, and suitable for retreat— just as you and your teacher are now?”
“I have heard this, Bhante, from aged and elderly wanderers, the teachers of teachers, as they were speaking:

‘Those who were the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, in the past, those Blessed Ones did not, having come together and gathered, dwell making a clamor, a loud noise, and a great din, intent upon various kinds of worldly talk—such as talk of kings, talk of thieves...
or talk of whether things exist or do not exist.’”
Just as I am now with my teacher,
so too did those Blessed Ones resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats— places of little noise,
little sound, secluded from people, hidden away from men, and suitable for seclusion— just as I do.
“‘The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma for awakening now.
But did it not occur to you, Nigrodha, being as wise and elderly as you are:
‘That Blessed One is a Buddha; he teaches the Dhamma for awakening. That Blessed One is self-tamed; he teaches the Dhamma for taming?’”
“Is it true that ‘the Blessed One is at peace and teaches the Dhamma for the sake of peace; the Blessed One has crossed over and teaches the Dhamma for the sake of crossing over;
the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna and teaches the Dhamma for the sake of final Nibbāna’?
5. The Realization of the Culmination of the Holy Life.
When this was said, the wanderer Nigrodha said to the Blessed One:
“A transgression overcame me, venerable sir, as foolish, deluded, and unwholesome as I was, in that I spoke thus to the Blessed One.
May the Blessed One accept my confession of that transgression for the sake of future restraint.”
“Truly, Nigrodha, a transgression has overcome you, as befitted one who is foolish, deluded, and unskilled, in that you spoke to me in such a way.
But since you, Nigrodha, having seen your transgression as a transgression, make amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it from you.

For this, Nigrodha, is growth in the discipline of the Noble Ones: when one sees a transgression as a transgression, makes amends for it in accordance with the Dhamma, and undertakes restraint for the future.”
But as for me, Nigrodha, I say this:
"Let a wise man—devoid of deceit, devoid of guile, and upright by nature—come; I instruct him, I teach him the Dhamma.
Practicing in accordance with what has been instructed—for whatever purpose sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness..."

They go forth, and in seven years he will, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Let alone seven years, Nigrodha.
"Let a wise man, free from deceit and guile, upright by nature, come; I instruct him, I teach him the Dhamma.

Practicing according to my instruction, he will, in this very life, through his own direct knowledge, realize for himself that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness."
Having attained it, he will dwell [in it] for six years;
for five years… for four years…
For three years...
for two years...
for one year.
"Let it be, Nigrodha, for one year.
Let a wise man—one who is not deceitful, not fraudulent, and upright by nature—come; I shall instruct him, I shall teach him the Dhamma.
Practicing according to that instruction—for what purpose sons of good family rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness—"
...go forth, and within seven months he will realize for himself with direct knowledge, attain, and dwell in that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life, having seen it in this very life.
Let alone seven months, Nigrodha...
For six months...
for five months...
for four months...
For three months … for two months … for one month …
For half a month.
Let alone half a month, Nigrodha.
Let a wise man—honest, free from deceit, and upright by nature—come; I shall instruct him, I shall teach him the Dhamma.

Practicing exactly as instructed, he will, in this very life, through his own direct knowledge, realize and dwell in the attainment of that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—
even within seven days.’
6. The Wanderers’ Reflection:
“It might occur to you, Nigrodha, that the ascetic Gotama says this out of a desire for disciples.”
But this, Nigrodha, should not be viewed in such a way.
Let him who is your teacher remain your teacher.
It may be, Nigrodha, that you think thus:
‘The ascetic Gotama says this because he wishes to divert us from our teaching.
But, Nigrodha, you should not view it in that way.
Let your teaching remain exactly as it is.
It may be, Nigrodha, that you think:
"The ascetic Gotama says this because he wishes to make us abandon our livelihood.
But, Nigrodha, it should not be viewed in this way.
"Whatever may be your way of livelihood, let that indeed remain your way of livelihood.
But it might occur to you, Nigrodha, thus:
'The ascetic Gotama says this because he wishes to establish us in those things which are unwholesome and reckoned as unwholesome by our teachers.'"
But this, Nigrodha, should not be viewed in such a way.
Let those things be unwholesome for you and reckoned as unwholesome by your teachers.
Now, Nigrodha, it might occur to you:
‘The ascetic Gotama says this because he wishes to separate us from those qualities that are wholesome and reckoned as wholesome by our teachers.
But it should not be viewed in this way, Nigrodha.
Let those qualities of yours remain wholesome and be reckoned as wholesome by your teachers.
Thus, Nigrodha, I do not speak thus out of a desire for discipleship; nor do I speak thus wishing to cause you to fall away from your recitation;

nor do I speak thus wishing to cause you to fall away from your livelihood; nor do I speak thus wishing to establish you in those things which are unwholesome and reckoned as unwholesome among your teachers; nor [do I speak thus] regarding those things which are wholesome and reckoned as wholesome.
Nigrodha, wishing to separate you from those who have teachers, I say this:

"There are indeed unwholesome states, Nigrodha, that have not been abandoned—states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—for the abandoning of which I teach the Dhamma.
By practicing accordingly, your defiling states will be abandoned and your purifying states will increase."
“Having realized for yourselves through direct knowledge in this very life the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom, you shall enter upon and abide in that state.
When this was said, those wanderers sat silent, ashamed, with shoulders slumped and heads downcast, brooding and speechless, as if their minds were possessed by Māra.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“All these foolish men have been touched by the Evil One.
For it seems that not even one among them will think:
‘Come now, let us live the holy life under the ascetic Gotama even for the sake of knowledge; what can seven days do?’”
Then the Blessed One, having let out a lion’s roar in the Udumbarikā Park for Wanderers, rose up into the air and reappeared on Vulture Peak Mountain.
But the householder Sandhāna entered Rājagaha at that very moment.
Thus ends the second discourse, the Udumbarika Sutta.
